summary: Describes an encapsulation method for carrying network interconnect traffic over a Frame Relay backbone, covering both bridging and routing. It replaces RFC 1294 and RFC 1490. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2427 defines how a Frame Relay frame identifies the network data it carries. It covers routed protocols, bridged LAN frames, and address resolution over permanent virtual circuits.

subtitle: How Frame Relay frames identify and carry routed and bridged network traffic.

tldr.problem: A Frame Relay frame needs to identify the network protocol it carries so the receiving station can process the payload correctly.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2427 places routed or bridged traffic inside a Q.922 frame and uses an NLPID, sometimes followed by a SNAP header, to identify it.
tldr.outcome: This Internet Standard replaces RFC 1294 and RFC 1490. It defines common encapsulations for IP, other routed protocols, bridging, and address resolution over permanent virtual circuits.

today: RFC 2427 is an Internet Standard published in September 1998. It obsoletes RFC 1490 and RFC 1294.

sections.title: Scope and Frame Relay Circuits
sections.content:
RFC 2427 specifies encapsulation for end stations that send routed or bridged traffic over a Frame Relay network. It applies to public and private networks and to switched and permanent virtual circuits; it does not specify the general behavior of the network equipment.

A virtual circuit connects stations. Its Data Link Connection Identifier (DLCI) is meaningful at a local interface in most networks, so the same circuit can have different identifiers at its ends. A station that supports multiple encapsulations must know which circuits use each one, and this encapsulation is used only on circuits configured for it.
sections.plainLanguage: This document tells devices at the ends of a Frame Relay connection how to package network traffic. Each end may use a different local number for the same connection.

sections.title: The Outer Frame
sections.content:
Each packet is carried in a Q.922 Annex A frame. Between its opening and closing flags, the frame has a Q.922 address, a control field, an optional pad, a Network Level Protocol ID (NLPID), the data, and a two-octet Frame Check Sequence. The usual control value is Unnumbered Information (UI), 0x03; Exchange Identification (XID) values are also permitted.

The address is usually two octets and contains a 10-bit Data Link Connection Identifier (DLCI), but it may use three or four octets. A pad, when present, is one zero octet and aligns the data. Value 0x00 is invalid because it cannot be distinguished from padding. A network must support a maximum frame size of at least 262 octets, and Data Terminal Equipment (DTE) must allow its accepted maximum to be configured.
sections.plainLanguage: The outer frame has an address, a control value, a protocol label, the data, and an error-check value. The NLPID tells the receiver how to interpret the data that follows.

sections.title: Routed and Bridged Traffic
sections.content:
A routed packet uses its assigned NLPID when one exists. For example, IPv4 uses 0xCC, while ISO CLNP uses 0x81. If a routed protocol has no NLPID, the sender uses NLPID 0x80 followed by a Subnetwork Access Protocol (SNAP) header. The SNAP header contains a three-octet Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI) and a two-octet Protocol Identifier (PID); OUI 0x00-00-00 means the PID is an Ethertype.

Bridged LAN frames also use NLPID 0x80, followed by SNAP with OUI 0x00-80-C2. The PID identifies the LAN frame format and whether its original Frame Check Sequence is preserved. The selected PID also identifies bridge protocol data units and source-routing bridge protocol data units.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver first reads a short protocol code. If the protocol has no code of its own, a SNAP header supplies an organization code and a protocol identifier.

sections.title: Negotiating Link Parameters
sections.content:
Stations may use the Q.922 Exchange Identification (XID) procedure when a circuit starts. It can negotiate the maximum frame size, retransmission timer, and maximum number of outstanding information frames. A station that does not support acknowledged multiple-frame operation sets the window size K to zero.

Without XID, the endpoints configure these values by agreement or use the Q.922 defaults: N201 is 260 octets and T200 is 1.5 seconds. The default K depends on link speed. A station supporting XID must answer an XID frame, and it reduces its frame size before replying if the remote limit is smaller.
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends can agree on frame size and retransmission settings when the circuit starts. Without that exchange, they must use agreed settings or the stated defaults.

sections.title: Address Resolution on Permanent Circuits
sections.content:
For a permanent virtual circuit, the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) can be carried in a SNAP frame with PID 0x0806. The Frame Relay hardware type is 15, and the hardware address is the Q.922 address. Because a DLCI is often local to one interface, the sender cannot necessarily place its own outgoing DLCI in the ARP message.

The Frame Relay network changes the DLCI as a frame crosses it. On receipt, the station copies the source address from the frame header into the ARP sender hardware-address field. The RFC describes the same approach for Reverse Address Resolution Protocol (RARP). In the absence of suitable multicast, a station can send a copy of an ARP request on each relevant circuit. Inverse ARP is not required by this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: ARP learns which circuit reaches another protocol address. The receiving station uses the circuit address in the arriving frame, because the sender's local circuit number may not be valid at the other end.

sections.title: Bridging Across Frame Relay
sections.content:
The bridging model uses remote bridge groups and virtual bridge ports. Every bridge in a group must have a full mesh of virtual circuits to the other bridges; otherwise, the network must use multiple groups. A virtual port may combine circuits into a LAN-like connection or treat each circuit as a separate point-to-point port.

With one virtual port for a group, the standard Spanning Tree Algorithm may be used. More than one virtual port in a group requires the extended algorithm described by IEEE 802.1g. In the LAN view, broadcasts are sent over each relevant circuit and the bridge learns which DLCI reaches each MAC address.
sections.plainLanguage: Bridges can treat several circuits as one shared connection or treat each circuit separately. The chosen arrangement determines how they forward broadcasts and prevent loops.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The receiver must trust that the sender correctly identified the protocol inside the frame. The encapsulation gives the receiver no general way to confirm that identification.

ARP and RARP over Frame Relay have the same security limits as those address-resolution protocols elsewhere. ARP does not authenticate messages, so host impersonation is a known risk; this RFC adds no security mechanism to ARP or RARP.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiver accepts the protocol label supplied by the sender. ARP and RARP messages are not authenticated by this specification.
